The share of a population with a characteristic, from the census profile

Source: R/census.R
profshr.Rd

The share of a group with a characteristic of the 2021 Census Indigenous Population Profile (foster children among children, speakers of an Indigenous language, households needing major repairs, ...), with an approximate confidence interval that carries the long-form sample and the random rounding of the counts.

Usage

profshr(
  x,
  num,
  den = NULL,
  smpfrac = 0.25,
  deff = 1,
  conflvl = 0.95,
  roubase = 5
)

Arguments

x

A cnsprof.

num

The characteristic counted: its chaid, or its name exactly.

den

The characteristic it is a share of (id or name); default its parent.

smpfrac

The long-form sampling fraction (default 0.25); full-count characteristics use 1 whatever is given.

deff

Design effect (default 1).

conflvl

Confidence level of the share's limits (default 0.95).

roubase

The base of the random rounding (default 5, Statistics Canada's); 1 for counts that are not rounded.

Value

A data frame of class rmbl_profile_share with geo, dguid, residence, gender, age, group, numerator, denominator, estimate (percent), lower, upper, quality; ready for indgap and dstntst. plot() draws it.

Details

The share is the numerator's count over the denominator's (by default the numerator's parent in the profile's hierarchy), for each geography, gender, age group and group. Statistics Canada does not publish standard errors for the profile, so the interval is an approximation built from what is known about how the counts were made:

  • a long-form ("25% sample") count is estimated from a sample of about one household in four, so the share has variance \(d (1 - f) p (1 - p) / (f N)\) for a sampling fraction \(f\) (smpfrac, 0.25) of a population of \(N\) (the denominator) and a design effect \(d\) (deff, 1 by default: the clustering of people in households raises it, and a value of 1.5 to 2 is prudent for characteristics shared within a household). On reserves (rows whose residence is "On reserve") every household got the long form, so \(f = 1\) there and the sampling term vanishes;

  • every count is randomly rounded, up or down without bias, to a multiple of \(b\) (roubase, 5). Averaged over the remainders, that adds variance \(c = (b^2 - 1)/6\) to each count (4 for \(b = 5\)), so \(c (1 + p^2) / N^2\) to the share (the only error of a full-count share).

In all, $$V = \frac{d (1 - f) p (1 - p)}{f N} + \frac{c (1 + p^2)}{N^2}.$$ The interval is Wilson's at the effective sample size \(n_e = \max(p(1-p), 1/N) / V\) (the floor \(1/N\) keeps a share of 0 or 100% from an infinite \(n_e\)), so it stays inside 0 and 100. It does not carry non-response (see tnrlf) or the edit and imputation error, so it is narrower than the full error; treat it as a lower bound on the uncertainty.

References

Statistics Canada (2022). Guide to the Census of Population, 2021, chapter 9 (data quality) and chapter 10 (confidentiality and random rounding). Catalogue no. 98-304-X.

Wilson EB (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association 22(158):209-212. doi:10.1080/01621459.1927.10502953

See also

cnsprof.

Examples

p <- cnsprof(indiex("censuspop"))
# children who are foster children, by province, First Nations, Metis, Inuit
# and non-Indigenous
fc <- profshr(p, "Foster children", "Total - Children in census families")
fc <- fc[
  fc$age == "0 to 14 years" &
    fc$group %in%
      c("First Nations", "M\u00e9tis", "Inuit", "Non-Indigenous"),
]
head(fc)
